items.q: Bounded blocking queue: how would you implement it with wait/notify and with Lock/Condition?
Printing in strict alternating order (print FooBar / print in order): what are the approaches and trade-offs?
Dining philosophers: which approaches prevent deadlock?
Read-heavy, write-light workloads: ReadWriteLock, StampedLock, or copy-on-write?
items.a:
**Proof labels — safety · ordering · visibility.**
ToolMechanismBest fit
synchronizedone thread at a timefrequent writes or a very short critical section
ReentrantReadWriteLockmultiple readers OR one writerreads ≫ writes and long critical sections
StampedLockadds lock-free optimistic readsextremely frequent reads and very rare writes
CopyOnWriteArrayListcopies the entire array on each writeextremely rare writes (listener lists)
**`StampedLock` — the standard optimistic-read pattern:** 
private final StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();
//
public double distanceFromOrigin() {
    long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead();      // acquire NO lock
    double cx = x, cy = y;                    // copy values into local variables
    if (!sl.validate(stamp)) {               // did a writer intervene?
        stamp = sl.readLock();               // yes => fall back to a real read lock
        try { cx = x; cy = y; } finally { sl.unlockRead(stamp); }
    }
    return Math.sqrt(cx * cx + cy * cy);
}
Optimistic read is not a read lock. Copy every field in the snapshot before validate; if validation fails, discard the entire local snapshot and reread under readLock. This is safe only for state protected by this StampedLock, not a transaction across unrelated state. The fast path performs no memory writes → it can be much faster than `ReadWriteLock` when writes are rare. The trade-off is that you must follow the pattern exactly: copy into local variables, call `validate`, and provide a fallback path. :::warn StampedLock is not reentrant Re-entering it can [[r:deadlock immediately]], unlike `synchronized` and `ReentrantLock`. It also does not support `Condition`. This is the main reason it should not be the default choice. ::: :::deep - `ReadWriteLock` is [[r:not]] always faster than `synchronized`. Its bookkeeping costs more, so `synchronized` wins for short critical sections of just a few lines. [[o:Measure it]]; do not guess. - Writer starvation: the default non-fair `ReentrantReadWriteLock` can admit readers continuously while a writer waits indefinitely. `new ReentrantReadWriteLock(true)` fixes that at the cost of throughput. - You can [[g:downgrade]] (write → read), but you [[r:cannot upgrade]] (read → write). Upgrading is a classic deadlock when two readers both attempt it. - A write to `CopyOnWriteArrayList` is O(n) and creates garbage. It is ideal for listener lists that are populated at startup and read forever, but a [[r:disaster]] for lists that change continuously. - A copy-on-write iterator captures a snapshot at creation time: iteration never throws `ConcurrentModificationException`, but it also does not observe later changes. State that semantic explicitly. - Often, [[g:the best lock is no lock]]: use `ConcurrentHashMap`, `AtomicReference` + `updateAndGet`, or an immutable snapshot swapped with a single volatile assignment. - Copy-on-write allocates a new backing array O(n) for each mutation. Old snapshots may remain live while iterators or readers use them, so memory and GC pressure depend on element count, write bursts, and retained iterators. Measure allocation and write latency; read-heavy alone is not enough. - Test optimistic reads while writers mutate, validate before using composite values, and verify the fallback path. Test that a copy-on-write iterator sees its creation-time snapshot, then measure allocation under a write burst. :::

items.q: CompletableFuture: how do you correctly make parallel calls, handle failures, and enforce timeouts?
items.a:
A common interview prompt: *"A booking page must call three services (pricing, seat availability, and promotions). How do you run them in parallel so total latency is determined by the slowest service?"* **Proof labels — safety · liveness · visibility.** The safety boundary is one result contract per request; liveness is bounded completion and cancellation; visibility follows the future and executor handoff. Failure policy must be explicit at the fan-in point. 
CompletableFuture<Price> price =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> priceApi.get(id), pool)
        .orTimeout(800, MILLISECONDS)              // Java 9+
        .exceptionally(e -> Price.unavailable());   // degrade gracefully; do not fail the entire page
//
CompletableFuture<Seats> seats =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> seatApi.get(id), pool)
        .orTimeout(800, MILLISECONDS)
        .exceptionally(e -> Seats.unknown());
//
// allOf waits for every stage; the subsequent join() calls no longer block in practice
CompletableFuture<Page> page = CompletableFuture
    .allOf(price, seats)
    .thenApply(v -> new Page(price.join(), seats.join()));
**Methods you must distinguish:** - `thenApply` (synchronous transformation) vs `thenCompose` (chain another future — [[o:effectively flatMap]]) - `thenCombine` (combine **two** futures) vs `allOf` (wait for **many**) vs `anyOf` (take the first to complete) - `exceptionally` (runs only on failure) vs `handle` (runs on success or failure) vs `whenComplete` (observes the outcome without transforming it) :::warn Three traps you must know [[r:Using ForkJoinPool.commonPool()]] for I/O can saturate a resource [[o:shared across the JVM]]. Its default parallelism is often available processors minus one, but runtime configuration and container limits can differ. Inspect it; use an owned I/O pool. ::: [[r:Calling `get()`/`join()` too early]] in the chain turns asynchronous work into sequential work and eliminates the benefit. [[r:Swallowing exceptions]]: without `exceptionally`/`handle`, the failure remains in the future until `join()` surfaces it, wrapped in `CompletionException`. :::deep - `thenApply` vs `thenApplyAsync`: the non-`Async` variant may run on [[o:the thread that completes the preceding stage]]. If that is Netty's I/O thread, you have just occupied the event loop. Heavy work belongs in the `Async` variant with a dedicated pool. - `orTimeout` (Java 9+) completes the future exceptionally with `TimeoutException`; `completeOnTimeout` supplies a default value. The latter is often the better degradation policy. - A `CompletableFuture` timeout [[r:does not cancel the underlying HTTP call]]; its thread can continue running to completion. You must also configure a timeout at the client layer (18-query-optimization.rewriting-the-query-reshaping-the-model.q4). - `allOf` returns `CompletableFuture<Void>`. To obtain the results, `join()` each constituent future afterward; that is safe because they have completed. - Failures are wrapped in `CompletionException`. Use `ex.getCause()` when classifying them; this is easy to forget. - Context such as MDC, trace IDs, and SecurityContext [[r:does not propagate automatically]] to another thread. Wrap the executor (for example, with Spring's `TaskDecorator`), or logs will lose their trace ID (20-observability-sre.slos-alerting-incidents.q4). - Java 21+: for I/O, [[g:virtual threads plus sequential code]] are often far clearer than a `CompletableFuture` chain (23-java-concurrency-coding.async-the-modern-toolkit.q4). Mentioning this shows that your concurrency model is current. - Exception policy belongs at fan-in. If degraded values are not acceptable, keep raw futures, use handle to collect outcome records, and make the aggregate preserve the root causes. allOf does not cancel siblings. - orTimeout only completes the stage. Keep a handle to the HTTP client's request or Future, configure a client-level deadline, and close or cancel that resource on timeout. Future.cancel(true) is only an interrupt request; test that the I/O stops and releases sockets. - The executor is an owned resource: use a bounded executor for the blocking workload, define rejection or degradation when full, and shut it down after its lifecycle. Never shut down an executor shared by other callers. - Test one fast failure, one slow child, timeout, and caller cancellation; assert the slow client is closed and no late side effect remains after the page future completes. :::

items.q: CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, Semaphore, and Phaser: how do they differ?
items.a:
These four synchronization tools are often asked about back-to-back because they are easy to confuse. **Proof labels — safety · liveness · visibility.** The safety property is the intended phase or permit state; liveness requires every participant to reach a terminal phase or be cancelled; synchronizer memory effects provide visibility across the handoff.
ToolPurposeReusableWho waits for whom
CountDownLatchwait for N tasks to finish before proceedingno — one-shotone or more waiters await N events
CyclicBarrierrendezvous N threads at one pointyes — resets automaticallythe threads wait for one another
Semaphorelimit concurrent entrantsyesthreads wait for permits
Phasera barrier whose party count can changeyes, across multiple phasesflexible
**`CountDownLatch` — accept traffic only after startup completes:** 
CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(3);
//
pool.submit(() -> { loadCache();  ready.countDown(); });
pool.submit(() -> { warmPool();   ready.countDown(); });
pool.submit(() -> { loadConfig(); ready.countDown(); });
//
if (!ready.await(30, SECONDS)) throw new IllegalStateException("startup timed out");
**`CyclicBarrier` — round-based simulation, with every participant meeting after each round:** 
CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(4, () -> mergeRoundResults());
// each worker has finished computing one round
barrier.await();     // the last worker to arrive runs mergeRoundResults()
:::deep - The key distinction: `CountDownLatch` [[o:cannot be reset]]. For repeated coordination, create a new latch or use `CyclicBarrier`/`Phaser`. This is the most common comparison question. - `countDown()` [[g:must]] be in a `finally` block; otherwise, one task throwing an exception can leave everyone waiting forever. - `await()` [[g:should always have a timeout]]. Waiting indefinitely in a production service is a recipe for hanging the entire system. - `CyclicBarrier` throws [[r:`BrokenBarrierException`]] for *every* participant when one thread is interrupted or times out. This is deliberate: without the full group, the round is meaningless. - `Semaphore` limits [[o:concurrency]] (for example, at most 10 simultaneous calls to a partner). This is a manual bulkhead, not rate limiting, which limits work over time (22.3). - `Phaser` is powerful but less common: the number of registered parties can change between phases (`register`/`arriveAndDeregister`), which suits multi-stage computations whose workers join and leave. - Java 21+: [[g:`StructuredTaskScope`]] can replace most "run several tasks, then wait" use cases more safely by canceling siblings automatically when one branch fails (23-java-concurrency-coding.async-the-modern-toolkit.q4). - Exercise the failure lifecycle: make one worker throw before countDown, interrupt a barrier waiter, exhaust semaphore permits, and add or remove Phaser parties. Every test needs a timeout and must verify that no worker remains blocked. :::

items.q: Atomics and CAS: how do you implement a lock-free counter/stack, and what is the ABA problem?
Virtual threads (Java 21+): how do they change the way you write concurrency code?
Interview drill: 20 threads each add one million to a `volatile int counter`. Is the total right, and how do you prove your answer?
items.a:
**Proof labels — safety · visibility.** The safety question is whether each increment is an atomic compound action; volatile supplies visibility and ordering only. The proof must cover every interleaving, not one benchmark result. No guarantee. The maximum is [[r:20,000,000]], and that result is possible when increments happen without overlapping. With concurrent read-modify-write interleavings, lost updates can make the result smaller; volatile provides visibility and ordering, not atomicity. `counter++` is three bytecodes: read the field, add one, write it back. Two threads that read the same value both write back `v + 1`, so one increment disappears. `volatile` guarantees each read sees a value from the synchronization order; it never fuses the three steps into one. 
static volatile int counter = 0;
// 20 threads x 1_000_000 increments
try (var pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20)) {
    for (int t = 0; t < 20; t++)
        pool.submit(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) counter++; });
}
System.out.println(counter);   // e.g. 3_147_882 — lower is possible; 20_000_000 is possible too, so one run proves nothing
**The fix ladder, cheapest correct option first:**
ToolUse whenWhat it costs
`AtomicInteger`one counter, moderate contentionCAS retries, all on one cache line
`LongAdder`write-heavy counter, read rarelystriped cells; `sum()` is not a snapshot while writes continue
`synchronized` / locktwo or more fields must move togetherblocking; keeping the critical section small is on you
no sharing at allper-thread totals combined at the endnothing — this is why reduce and collect scale
:::warn What volatile is actually for Publication, not accumulation: a `stop` flag, a swapped configuration reference — state whose every invariant fits inside one atomic read or one atomic write (01-java-core-jvm.memory-execution-model.q1). ::: :::deep **"Run it and look" is a weak proof.** A lost update is timing-dependent, and a JIT-optimised loop on an idle laptop can print the right number while proving nothing. Two stronger arguments: - *by construction* — name the three steps and the interleaving that drops one; no measurement makes that safe - *by tooling* — jcstress, the OpenJDK concurrency harness, drives the interleavings and reports the outcomes actually observed, including ones a plain test never reaches **Atomics do not make compound actions atomic either.** `if (counter.get() < limit) counter.incrementAndGet()` is the same bug one level up: use `compareAndSet` in a loop, `updateAndGet`, or a lock (23-java-concurrency-coding.async-the-modern-toolkit.q3). **Watch the read side too.** Incrementing under a lock is correct, but reading the field from another thread without that lock is a fresh visibility problem — the fix has to cover both sides of the field, which is exactly what `AtomicInteger` gives you in one object. **Test hooks.** A jcstress test with Actor methods and an Arbiter can record allowed outcomes for the race; a stress test can expose loss but cannot prove its absence. For an exact total, use AtomicInteger, a lock, or per-thread ownership followed by a final reduction. :::

items.q: How do you design cancellation and backpressure for async fan-out without orphan work?
items.a:
Start with the resource contract, not with `CompletableFuture.allOf`. Fan-out must have a parent deadline, a bounded admission policy, an explicit executor owner, and a rule for what happens to children when the caller leaves. **Proof labels — safety · liveness · ordering · visibility.** The safety property is no work or side effect after scope closure; liveness is bounded completion and cancellation; ordering covers deadline and admission propagation; visibility follows the owned cancellation state.
ConcernRequired decisionFailure to test
AdmissionBound concurrency with a semaphore, bounded executor/queue, or structured scope; reject or degrade explicitlyUnbounded fan-out exhausts CPU, sockets, DB connections or provider quota
DeadlineCarry one monotonic deadline into each child and subtract elapsed timeEach child gets a fresh timeout and total latency exceeds the request budget
Failure policyChoose fail-fast, best-effort aggregation, or partial result; preserve the first/root causeOne failure is hidden behind an aggregate exception or partial side effects are mistaken for success
CancellationDefine whether cancellation interrupts the task, closes the I/O, releases permits, and prevents retries`orTimeout` completes a future while the underlying supplier keeps running
LifecycleOwn and shut down executors; do not leak work into the common pool or a request-scoped executorOrphan tasks survive deploy/shutdown and continue writing after the response timed out
:::deep - `CompletableFuture.orTimeout` changes completion of the future; it is not a proof that arbitrary blocking I/O stopped. The adapter must own cancellation/close semantics, and tests must observe the resource after timeout. - `allOf` does not decide whether sibling tasks should be cancelled, whether their exceptions are collected, or whether side effects are safe to retry. Write that policy in code and documentation. - A semaphore limits admission but does not cancel work already admitted; a bounded queue creates a different latency/rejection contract. Measure queue age, permit wait, child p99 and cancellation lag. - `StructuredTaskScope` in the researched JDK 25 API is preview. It provides a useful lifetime model, but the selected compiler/runtime must opt in and the application still needs downstream bulkheads. - For mutations, cancellation may leave an unknown external outcome. Use an idempotency key and reconciliation boundary rather than blindly retrying a timed-out child. - Tests should cover deadline propagation, sibling cancellation, executor shutdown, interrupted/late completion, retry suppression, permit release and no work after the request scope closes. :::
